editorNote.lead: This chooser lists ou=policies, and two policies that are deciding right now are not in it. The issuance policy (what this service will issue) and the access policy (who reaches the console, the User Portal, SCIM, the SPIRE Server API) are BUILT IN — called at decision time rather than seeded — so there is no stored document for this editor to open.
editorNote.overridden: One or more of them HAS an override in the repository, so it is in the list above and opens here like any other policy.
editorNote.createBefore: Create one from its template on the
editorNote.label: Two policies are deciding and are not in this list
own.builtInDisabled: the built-in document — the entry {name} exists and is disabled
own.heading: What this service decides its own boundaries with
own.warn1: These two policies are IN FORCE and are not in the table above. That table is ou=policies; these are BUILT IN — the template is called at decision time rather than seeded into the repository — so the editor has never listed them and a reader looking only at the repository would conclude that whatever is root there is what this service enforces. Usually it is not: a seeded example policy decides nothing this service does.
own.warn2: They are built in rather than seeded on purpose. ou=policies is per trust realm, so a policy written once into the default realm leaves every realm created afterwards unable to decide anything at all — and falling back to the default realm's copy would couple two realms, which is the one thing the realm design does not do. Called rather than seeded, every realm has both of them out of the box with nothing to delete.
own.warn3: An override is an ordinary policy. Create one from the same template, named whatever the setting says, and it wins from the next request — it then appears in the table above and in the editor like everything else. Neither is sent to a remote PEP: GET /xacml/pep/policies carries the policies about somebody ELSE's boundary, and these two are about this service's own.
own.warnLabel: Two policies decide here and are not in the repository
noPeps.shared: That does not mean none is running: registering is not what lets a PEP enforce, and one that only ever pulls /xacml/pep/policies works perfectly and never appears here.
noPeps.anywhere: No remote Policy Enforcement Point has registered, in this realm or in any other.
noPeps.elsewhere: No remote Policy Enforcement Point has registered in this realm — but {n, plural, =1 {{n} other realm holds} other {{n} other realms hold}} one:
noPeps.perRealm: . The register is per realm, like the policy repository it serves, so a PEP that registered against /realm/<id> is listed there and nowhere else.
monitor.notReported: not reported — a remote PEP sends what it enforced, and only the process that EVALUATED knows which of the four decisions each was
monitor.notEnforced: nothing was enforced here — this service produced the decision and somebody else's PEP acted on it, in their process
pep.currentTip: This PEP reported holding the repository digest this service has now.
pep.notCurrentTip: The sync token this PEP last reported is not the one the repository has now. It converges on its next poll.
monitor.inProcessTip: Compiled into this process. It is running because this page is.
overview.noRootBefore: No policy is marked as the root, so every decision is NotApplicable. A PDP evaluates one document and reaches the rest through PolicyIdReference, so exactly one policy in the repository is where evaluation starts. Choose one on the
overview.p1: This service is a Policy Decision Point. It is the only protocol family here that answers a question about somebody else’s boundary: every other one authenticates or provisions a person, and this one is handed a subject who was authenticated somewhere else and asked whether they may.
overview.p2: Policies live in ou=policies in the embedded directory. That container is the repository rather than a copy of one, so an ldapmodify there changes what the PDP decides on the next request — and a policy survives a restart whenever persistence.mode is not memory.
overview.p3: The PIP reads attributes off the subject’s own directory entry, so a policy can grant on employeeType without the caller having to assert it. What the REQUEST carries wins over the directory, because a PEP asserting an attribute is describing that request while the directory is describing the world.
overview.label: What this page configures
policies.empty: The repository is empty, so every decision is NotApplicable. Create one from a template below.
template.name: Name for the policy
template.nameHelp: Names the directory entry. The PolicyId inside the document is separate and may be any URI.
policies.p1: ou=policies in the embedded directory is this table. An ldapmodify of xacmlPolicyDocument changes what the PDP decides on the next request, and xacmlEnabled takes a policy out of the decision without deleting it.
policies.p2: Exactly one policy is the root. A PDP evaluates one document and reaches the rest through PolicyIdReference, so the root is where evaluation starts. A repository with none decides nothing; one with two is refused rather than resolved arbitrarily.
policies.p3: A policy that does not type-check is shown in red here and was refused when it was written — XACML is statically typed, so such a policy is wrong for every request rather than for some.
th.name: Name
alfa.heading: Import ALFA
alfa.p1: ALFA is the readable syntax for XACML. Paste one here and it is parsed, converted and STORED AS XACML XML — the repository holds one representation, because two would be two things to keep in step.
alfa.p2: Every attribute must be DECLARED before it is used. That is ALFA's own rule and it is the most useful refusal in the parser: a typo in an attribute name is otherwise a policy that quietly matches nothing, which looks exactly like a policy that is working and denying you. Open any policy in the editor to see the shape.
alfa.label: What this accepts
template.heading: Create from a template
template.p1: A template is the first twenty clicks of the editor already made: a working, valid, evaluable policy in a shape people actually write. The editor takes it from there.
template.p2: blank is the exception and it is here on purpose. It makes no argument and there is nothing in it to read — an empty Policy, or an empty PolicySet, which is the only way to create one of those here without importing ALFA. It denies every request until you put a rule in it, because deny-unless-permit over nothing at all is a Deny. That is the direction a half-built policy should fail in, and it is why building it before making it the root is the right order.
template.p3: RBAC asks what role do you hold; ABAC asks what is true about you, this resource and right now. The first is what most deployments have and the second is what they wanted — having both here, producing documents in the same language, is the clearest way to see what the difference costs in policy.
template.label: What a template is
pep.staleTip: Nothing has been heard from this PEP for longer than xacml.pepStaleAfterS. It may still be enforcing — this service cannot tell.
pep.unauthenticatedNote: Registered with no client certificate, which xacml.pepRequireCertificate allowed. Nothing about this row is proven.
pep.noNotify: none — never nudged, and it converges on its own poll anyway
pep.notifyUnusable.host: unusable: the host is not on xacml.pepNotifyAllowedHosts
pep.notifyUnusable.http: unusable: plain http — the nudge is sent over HTTPS only
pep.notifyUsable: usable — nudged when the repository changes
pep.notifyDerived: derived by the PEP from its HTTPS listener certificate
pep.undischargeable: {n} of those refused for an obligation it could not discharge
peps.p1: A remote Policy Enforcement Point runs in another process, holds its own copy of this engine, pulls the enabled policies from /xacml/pep/policies and decides locally. That is the point of having one: a PEP that asked this service per request would be POST /xacml/pdp with a network hop in front of every access decision.
peps.p2: The pull is the contract. When the repository changes this service also POSTs a few bytes to each PEP that gave a notify URL, saying only that something changed. That is an optimisation over the polling interval and never a replacement for it — a nudge that is refused, blocked or never delivered costs one polling interval and nothing else, which is why the failure is worth showing here and not worth alarming about.
peps.p3: Nothing on this page reaches into another process. “Stop nudging” stops this service dialling that PEP; it does not stop it enforcing, because it already holds the engine and the policy. “Forget” removes the row. Neither takes a running enforcement point out of service, and a console that implied otherwise would be worse than one with no controls at all.
peps.p4: Registering is not a permission. An unregistered PEP can pull and enforce exactly as well; what a row buys is this page and an address for the nudge.
peps.sync: The repository’s sync token is {token}. {current} of {total} registered PEP(s) hold it; {stale} have not been heard from for {after}s.
peps.off: Remote Policy Enforcement Points are turned off (xacml.remotePeps), so the three endpoints under /xacml/pep answer 501 and nothing here is nudged. The register below is untouched and comes back when it is turned on.
peps.notifyOff: The nudge is turned off (xacml.pepNotify), so nothing below is dialled. Every PEP still converges on its own poll — that is what makes this safe to turn off.
peps.cert1: A remote PEP answers its own clients, and the column above is the certificate it answers them with. It is issued by the Remote PEP listeners Issuing CA of this realm — the realm the PEP registered to — so a client that installed this service’s Root CA verifies it, and the chain still says which realm vouched for that front door. It names the PEP’s registered name and the host of its notify URL, plus whatever you add.
peps.cert2: The private key is shown once, on the page that answers the button, and this service keeps no copy. Write the two blocks to the files the container reads (PEP_HTTPS_CERT and PEP_HTTPS_KEY); it picks up a pair written after it started, and reissuing supersedes the certificate it replaces on the issuer’s revocation list.
peps.numbers1: The decision counts are the PEP’s own, reported by it, cumulative in its process. This service did not see one of those decisions — that is what a remote PEP is — so a PEP that restarts makes its counts go down, which is honest rather than broken.
peps.numbers2: The bias column is likewise reported. A remote PEP’s bias is its own configuration (PEP_BIAS), and nothing on this service sets it; a control here that appeared to would silently do nothing.
monitor.hereWhat: Decisions THIS process made, counted as it happened. Since {since}.
monitor.remoteWhat: What registered Policy Enforcement Points in OTHER processes REPORT having done, on their heartbeats, cumulative in their own memory. This service saw none of it — that is what a remote PEP is — and a PEP that restarts makes this half go down.
monitor.combinedWhat: The two rows added up. It is the figure a deployment wants and it is arithmetic over two different kinds of evidence rather than a measurement, which is why it is a row here and not the only number on the page.
monitor.addUp: Allowed + refused + not-enforced = decisions, on every row. The third column is the one that is easy to be surprised by and it is not a failure: it counts the decisions POST /xacml/pdp produced for somebody ELSE’s enforcement point. This service evaluated them and never saw what was done with the answers, so counting them as allowed or refused would be reporting an enforcement it was not present for.
monitor.addUpLabel: Why the three do not add to the total on their own
monitor.p1: This is the only page in this family about traffic. The others are about configuration — what policies exist, what one of them says, what the PDP would decide about a subject you type in. This one answers the question you have when authorization is misbehaving: how many decisions are being made, by which enforcement point, and how many of them are refusals.
monitor.p2: “Decisions” and “allows” are not two views of one tally. XACML has FOUR decisions — Permit, Deny, NotApplicable, Indeterminate — and a PEP has TWO outcomes. What maps between them is the PEP’s bias: a deny-biased PEP refuses a NotApplicable and a permit-biased one allows it, from the same decision on the same request. And an obligation a PEP cannot discharge turns a Permit into a refusal (section 7.2) — the one enforcement outcome that looks like a bug from the client side and is the specification working. So allowed is not permit, and both are drawn.
monitor.p3before: The counters are in memory and start when this process does. They are observations, and this service persists nothing it observes; the durable record of a refusal is the
monitor.p3after: , which holds the reason as well as the count. They are also per trust realm, like ou=policies itself — this page is showing {realm}, and a decision made under another realm was made against another realm’s policies.
monitor.p4: There is no reset button, deliberately: a console that could zero its own monitoring would make every number here a number somebody might have zeroed. A restart is what clears them.
monitor.off: The XACML family is switched off (xacml.enabled), so nothing is being evaluated and every figure below has stopped moving. The embedded PEPs answer ALLOWED without asking the PDP — which is what keeps a service with the family off a smaller service rather than a broken one — and those allows are counted, because they are what happened.
monitor.list1: An embedded PEP is not “registered” and cannot be. It is compiled into this process, so its existence is a fact about the build rather than something it told this service; there are exactly two and they are the catalogue in xacml_monitor.js. A remote PEP registers because it has no other way to be known about — and even that is not a permission: an unregistered PEP can pull /xacml/pep/policies and enforce perfectly, and never appears here. So this list is every enforcement point this service KNOWS ABOUT, which is a smaller claim than every one that exists, and the difference cannot be closed from this end.
monitor.list2: No PEP’s bias is settable here. The issuance and access PEPs are deny-biased by construction — an issuance or an access that was not permitted does not happen — and a remote PEP’s bias is reported by it, because a control here that appeared to set another process’s bias would silently do nothing.
monitor.list3before: The remote rows are a summary.
monitor.list3after: has the sync tokens, the notify URLs, what happened to the last nudge, and the controls.
monitor.listLabel: What this list is, and what it is not
monitor.refusal1before: A refusal here is a policy decision and the reason is in the
monitor.refusal1after: , not in this table: xacml.issuance.refused for the issuance PEP and xacml.access.refused for the access PEP. This page says how many; that log says who, what and why.
monitor.refusal2before: To make a decision happen on purpose and watch it land here, use
monitor.refusal2after: — but note that the enforcement preview on that page is deliberately not counted. It is a what-if rather than a request anybody guarded, and counting it would make this page’s numbers grow every time somebody looked at it. A remote PEP’s GET /protected is where a request you make on purpose is really enforced.
monitor.refusal3: Drawing THIS page adds one to the access PEP's count, and that is right rather than a measurement artefact. /admin is one of the five gated surfaces, so reading it is a real request that the access policy really decided — the number would be wrong if it did not move. It is the opposite case from the preview above, and the two are worth telling apart: one is an access that happened, the other is a question somebody typed.
decide.subject: Subject
decide.subjectHelp: A name, a DN or a certificate subject — all three resolve the way they do everywhere else here. The PIP reads this person’s directory entry for any attribute the policy asks for.
decide.resourceHelp: Optional. Becomes resource-id, as an anyURI.
decide.noneApplied: none — nothing in the repository applied
decide.p1: The decision is the PDP’s and the outcome is the PEP’s, and this page shows both because they are not the same answer. A deny-biased PEP refuses an Indeterminate and a permit-biased one allows it; the two agree on every Permit and every Deny. When somebody says a policy “is not working”, it is nearly always because only one of these two was being looked at.
decide.p2: Nothing here asserts an attribute in the request beyond the subject, the action and the resource — so anything else the policy needs comes from the PIP, off that person’s directory entry. That is what makes this a test of the whole path rather than of the engine alone.
decide.label: What you are looking at
editor.emptyBefore: The repository is empty, so there is nothing to edit.
editor.creatingBefore: Creating a policy happens on the
editor.emptyAfter: , in one of three ways: from a template, by importing ALFA, or from the blank template — an empty document with nothing in it, which is the starting point for writing one here rather than editing one somebody else shaped. Come back to this page with it and every element goes in from the menus below.
editor.where1: This editor changes a policy that already exists, and the chooser above is every policy in the repository.
editor.where1after: — there is no New button here, because every control on this page names a stored document and a path inside it, and a policy nobody has written yet has neither.
editor.where2: Three doors on that page: a template (a working policy in a shape people actually write, which is the first twenty clicks of this editor already made), Import ALFA (paste the readable syntax and it is stored as XACML XML), and the blank template — a Policy with no rules or a PolicySet with no policies, for writing one here from nothing. A blank document denies every request until you put something in it, because deny-unless-permit over no rules at all is a Deny; that is the safe direction for a half-built policy to fail in, but it is worth knowing before making one the root.
editor.whereLabel: Where a new policy comes from
editor.liveBefore: This policy is enabled and is the root, so it is what the PDP is deciding with right now. There is no draft state in this editor — the draft IS the stored policy, and every change below takes effect on the next request. That is deliberate: nothing can be lost by closing the browser, and there is no second copy that could disagree with the stored one. To work on it safely, disable it first on the
xpath.one: This document holds an AttributeSelector or an xpathExpression value, and {name} declares no XPathVersion
xpath.many: This document holds an AttributeSelector or an xpathExpression value, and these declare no XPathVersion
xpath.rest: . Section 5.14 says the element MUST be present when a policy uses one. Nothing here will refuse the document — this PDP has one XPath engine and does not choose a dialect by URI, so the decision is the same either way — but a schema validator elsewhere will refuse it, and this is the kind of defect that travels a long way before anybody finds out. The field is on the policy's own row above: http://www.w3.org/TR/1999/REC-xpath-19991116 is what the conformance suite uses.
xpath.label: No XPathVersion, and this document needs one
editor.typeCheck: XACML is statically typed, so these are wrong for every request rather than for some. The policy is stored, but it will not load — the PDP reports Indeterminate and names the first problem.
how.p1: Each row is one element of the policy. The Add dropdown beside it offers exactly what XACML allows at that point and nothing else — a Match may only go inside an alternative, a Condition only on a rule and only one per rule, and the function list on a Match is the two-argument boolean predicates rather than all 275 functions.
how.p2before: Those menus are computed on the server, by the same code that validates the policy, against the real function library — so the editor cannot offer you something that will then be refused. This console runs under script-src 'none' and has no JavaScript anywhere, which is why every control is a form and every choice is a round trip. The cost is real: a five-rule policy built by hand is perhaps forty of them. The templates on the
how.p2after: page are the first twenty already made.
how.p3: Every element you add arrives complete and valid — a new rule has a Target and an Effect, a new Match has a function, a value and an attribute. An editor that produced half-built elements would hold a document that could not be saved, and a document that cannot be saved cannot be evaluated, which is when you most want to look at it.
how.p4: A PolicySet is edited here too, and it holds policies rather than rules. Its children may be a policy written inline, a nested set, or a PolicyIdReference naming a policy stored separately in this repository — which is how a PDP reaches more than one document: the root is evaluated and references are resolved when a decision is made. Its combining algorithm comes from the policy-combining list, which is a different set of URIs from the rule-combining one they are almost spelt the same as.
how.p5: The rest of the syntax is here as well: VariableDefinition (named once, evaluated once per request, visible to its own policy only), AttributeSelector (an XPath over a request category’s content, with the namespace bindings its prefixes need), Function as a value (what a higher-order function such as any-of or map takes as its first argument), the attribute assignments under an obligation, and the optional attributes — Version, Issuer, MustBePresent, ContextSelectorId, XPathVersion and MaxDelegationDepth.
how.p6: Two things are shown and cannot be added. The four combiner-parameter elements are drawn and removable, because a document may arrive carrying them and an element you cannot see is one you cannot delete — but there is no Add button, since section C of the specification says none of the twelve standard combining algorithms takes a parameter, and a control that provably changes no decision would be the first such control on this console. <PolicyIssuer> is not here at all: it belongs to the administrative delegation profile, which this PDP does not implement, so a document carrying one loses it here.
how.label: How this editor works
editor.alfa1: ALFA — the Abbreviated Language For Authorization — is the third rendering of this policy and the one worth reading. Forty lines of XML are eight of ALFA and the eight say the same thing.
editor.alfa2: It is an OASIS Committee Specification Draft rather than a ratified standard: there is no conformance suite for it and no second implementation to disagree with. So the contract here is the one that can actually be kept — anything this emits, it reads back, and the policy decides identically either way — and not that it reads every ALFA document in the world.
form.policyHelp: Version is dot-separated numbers. MaxDelegationDepth is carried and not honoured — this PDP implements no administrative delegation, so the attribute survives a round trip and is read by nothing. XPathVersion belongs in <{defaults}> and the specification asks for it whenever the document holds an AttributeSelector or an xpathExpression.
form.referenceHelp: The id of a policy stored separately in this repository. It is resolved when a decision is made rather than when this document is loaded, so naming one that does not exist yet is allowed — an unresolved reference is reported on the decision. Leave Version empty for no constraint.
form.variableHelp: Every VariableReference naming it is rewritten with it — a rename that left them behind would produce a document that does not load, and the write would be refused. The scope is this policy: a sibling policy in the same set cannot see it.
form.matchType: The datatype follows the function — both sides become {type}.
form.matchHelp: A Match holds an AttributeDesignator or an AttributeSelector and never both. Switching the kind redraws this form with the fields that kind takes. Must be present is the difference between an absent attribute being an empty bag and being Indeterminate — which is the difference between a policy that quietly does not apply and one that fails closed.
form.assignmentHelp: What the PEP is handed alongside the obligation. Category and Issuer are optional and mean "this assignment is about that category" — leave them empty for a plain named value. The value itself is the expression below.
form.xpathHelp: An xpathExpression value is an XPath, and XPathCategory is the request category it runs against. The prefix bindings it uses travel with the document.
form.issuerHelp: An empty Issuer means any issuer, which is not the same as an issuer whose name is the empty string — so clearing the box removes the attribute rather than writing one.
form.selectorHelp: An AttributeSelector runs an XPath over the <Content> of a request category and returns a bag, exactly as a designator does — so most functions still need a one-and-only around it. ContextSelectorId names an attribute holding the node to start from; empty means the whole content.
form.bindingsHelp: . A prefix in the path means nothing without one, and they travel with the document. Type a prefix and a URI to add or change one; a prefix with an empty URI removes it.
form.functionHelp: Named here as a value rather than applied — this is the first argument of a higher-order function such as any-of, all-of or map. Applying it instead is the commonest way to write one of those wrongly.
form.undefinedVariable: Names ${name}, which this policy does not define — so the document will not load. Add a variable definition to the policy, or replace this expression from the Add menu.
form.scopeHelp: Only the variables this policy defines are offered. A VariableReference may not name one belonging to a sibling policy in the same set — section 5.24 — and the document would not load.
authzen.label: What this is
authzen.p1: The AuthZEN Authorization API answers one access question per request at /access/v1/evaluation, decided by this page's engine against the realm's root policy. Policies tell an AuthZEN question apart by urn:sts:xacml:protocol = authzen.
authzen.p2: A caller authenticates by authzen.callerAuthentication — a client certificate by default — must be a member of the group named by roles.authzenPepGroup (the AUTHZEN_PEPS role), and may ask only about the applications in its scope. A request property reaches the policy only through a catalogue row below; an undeclared one is refused.
authzen.noObject: This realm has no sts-authzen-api application, so the AuthZEN API answers 501 here and the catalogue has nowhere to live.
authzen.noRows: No property is declared, so a request carrying any property is refused.
authzen.reserved: Refused: anything in urn:sts:xacml:, subject-id, resource-id and action-id, context.application, and a bare directory attribute name in a subject category.
authzen.callersNote: The members of the group granting AUTHZEN_PEPS. A caller may name in context.application only an application in its scope; an application caller's own is always in it.
authzen.noScope: none — it may ask about nothing
authzen.noCallers: The group has no members, so nobody may call the AuthZEN API.
authzen.callbacksHeading: Set a caller's access request callback URLs
authzen.callbacksNote: An access request's callback.endpoint must be one of these exactly; this service never dials a callback URL taken from a request alone. https only, at most eight, separated by spaces or commas; empty clears them.
authzen.requestsNote: AuthZEN access requests (the Access Request and Approval Profile): a Deny whose answer carried the advice urn:sts:xacml:advice:access-request, submitted by the PEP. Deciding one is asked of the access-control policy (action approve-access-request), so its subject cannot approve it. An approval reaches the next evaluation only as trusted facts the root policy reads.
authzen.requestsOff: The profile is off in this realm (authzen.accessRequests).
authzen.requestStatus: {status, select, pending {pending} approved {approved} denied {denied} expired {expired} cancelled {cancelled} failed {failed} other {{status}}}
authzen.noRequests: No access request has been submitted in this realm.
fga.heading: Applications' own policies
fga.label: What this section is
fga.p1: Each application owns a fine-grained authorization policy that decides the RFC 9396 details of its own types. It is never the root, the remote PEPs are never sent it, and it is edited in the editor like any other policy.
fga.p2: A policy whose application was deleted is kept, disabled and marked orphaned, until it is removed here. The policy an application still names cannot be removed; reset it from the application's Fine-grained authorization tab.
fga.removeTip: Delete this policy. No application names it, so nothing decides with it.
fga.none: No application owns a policy in this realm.
proxy.label: Reverse proxy
proxy.p1: A registered remote PEP may stand in front of an application as a reverse proxy. It pulls this configuration over its mutual TLS, decides each request locally with this realm’s policies, and asks this service to validate what it cannot validate itself. A request no route matches is refused 404.
proxy.heading: Reverse proxy: {name}
proxy.none: No reverse-proxy configuration: this PEP’s proxy answers 404 to everything.
proxy.problem: The stored configuration does not validate, so it is not pulled:
proxy.disabled: Disabled: the proxy answers 404 to everything.
proxy.editNote: The routes are ordered and the first match wins: add a route by adding an object to routes, remove one by deleting it, reorder them by moving them. The whole document is validated when it is saved, and any part of it that is wrong is refused by name.
proxy.unusable: Not usable, so the proxy refuses this route:
proxy.identity.mode.saml: a signed SAML Response to the application
proxy.identity.mode.jwt: an access token for the application
proxy.identity.note: In headers mode, each row that names a header sends that claim (at most 16); leave a row empty to leave it unused. The SAML mode needs the application’s SAML entity ID and assertion consumer service; the token mode needs an audience. The whole configuration is checked again when it is saved.
proxy.signals.label: CAEP/RISC signal streams
proxy.signals.notReported: Signal-stream health: not reported. A PEP older than this service, or one whose proxy is off, sends none.
proxy.signals.none: No signal streams: no session route has signals on.
proxy.signals.summary: {receivers} stream(s): {healthy} healthy, {stale} stale (stale after {staleAfterMs} ms without a successful poll; polled every {pollIntervalMs} ms).
proxy.signals.staleNote: A stale stream’s routes ask this service’s session endpoint until it polls again.
proxy.signals.library: Library session stores: {held} held of {max} ({ttlSec} s lifetime), {evicted} evicted, {expired} expired.
pepPage.lead: Everything about one remote PEP: what it registered as, what it reports, its listeners, its reverse proxy, its signal streams and the settings this service sets for it. Nothing on this page reaches into the PEP's process: the PEP pulls what is changed here on its next poll.
pepPage.notFound: No remote PEP is registered as {name} in this realm.
pepPage.openRow: Open a PEP's name for its own page: its settings, its listeners, its reverse proxy and its signal streams.
pepPage.th.name: Name
pepSettings.applies.nextReload: at the next re-read of its HTTPS pair
pepSettings.bootstrap.heading: Set only in the PEP's environment
pepSettings.bootstrap.lead: These are the minimum the PEP needs to reach this service the first time, or they name something on its own container, so they cannot be set here.
pepSettings.current: The PEP has applied the settings set here.
pepSettings.inUseNotReported: This PEP has not reported its settings: it is older than them, or it has not sent a heartbeat since it started.
pepSettings.key.proxyRpAllowInsecure: Relying party may use an http issuer
pepSettings.key.proxyUpstreamInsecure: Do not verify an https upstream
pepSettings.key.resource: Resource when a request names none
pepSettings.key.timeoutMs: Timeout of a call to this service (ms)
pepSettings.lead: Each setting below may be set here, and the PEP pulls it from GET /xacml/pep/settings. The precedence is this page, then the PEP's environment variable, then its default: a box left empty is not set, so the PEP uses its environment for it, exactly as it did before this page existed.
pepSettings.lead2: A PEP older than these settings never asks for them and goes on using its environment. In use at the PEP is what the PEP last reported on a heartbeat, and where each value came from.
pepSettings.notCurrent: The PEP has not yet applied the settings set here; it does on its next pull.
pepSettings.problem: The settings stored for this PEP do not validate, so none is sent:
pepSettings.reason.bind: a port the PEP listens on; it is not rebound while it serves
pepSettings.reason.connect: needed to reach and authenticate to this service before the first pull
pepSettings.reason.file: a file on the PEP's own disk that its TLS stack reads
pepSettings.reason.listeners: whether the reverse proxy's listeners are started at all; the proxy configuration's own switch is set on the Reverse proxy tab
pepSettings.reason.narrowing: the operator's own narrowing of the AuthZEN callers this service sends
listeners.lead: Every listener this PEP has. The four its environment binds (PEP_PORT, PEP_HTTPS_PORT, PEP_PROXY_PORT, PEP_PROXY_HTTPS_PORT) are what lets it reach this service before it has pulled anything, so they are shown read-only and only its environment changes them.
listeners.lead2: Any number of further HTTP or HTTPS listeners, for the decision API or the reverse proxy, may be defined here. The PEP binds, rebinds and unbinds them on its next pull, without a restart, and reports what each is doing on its next heartbeat. An HTTPS listener's key is generated by the PEP, which asks this realm's Remote PEP listeners Issuing CA for its certificate; no private key ever reaches this service.
listeners.olderPep: This PEP does not report its listeners: it is older than listener reporting, so the state of each is unknown and the listeners defined here are not bound by it.
listeners.problem: The listeners stored for this PEP do not validate, so none is pulled:
listeners.reason.addressInUse: the address and port are in use
listeners.reason.permissionDenied: the PEP may not bind that port
listeners.reason.addressUnavailable: the address is not one of the PEP's
listeners.reason.certificateRefused: the certificate and key were not usable
listeners.reason.proxyOff: the PEP's reverse proxy is off (PEP_PROXY)
listeners.httpOffHow: Plain HTTP is off by default. Set {enable}=true in the PEP's environment to bind it on {port}, or define an HTTP listener on this tab.
listeners.reason.other: another failure; the PEP's log says which
listeners.reason.crlOnly: CRLs only (PEP_CRL_HTTP): the API answers on HTTPS
listeners.enableHint: Off unless {enable}=true is set in the PEP's environment (the default).
listeners.renewPending: a new certificate is asked for on the next pull
listeners.envOnly: set by {env} in the PEP's environment
listeners.cert.subject: Subject
listeners.plainProxyRefused: This realm is in product mode and xacml.pepPlainHttpProxyListeners is off, so a plain-HTTP reverse-proxy listener is refused.
listeners.form.httpsOnly: For an HTTPS listener: the names its certificate carries beside the PEP's own name and its notify host, and the key the PEP generates.
listeners.envPairLead: The two environment HTTPS listeners serve the pair on the PEP's own mount (PEP_HTTPS_CERT and PEP_HTTPS_KEY). Issue it here and write it there; the PEP picks it up without a restart.
proxy.signals.noRows: This PEP reports the streams' totals and not one row per stream: it is older than the per-stream report.
proxy.signals.unknownClient: a client this PEP's routes do not name
routeForm.lead: The form saves the whole configuration through the same checks as the document on the Manifest tab: the routes are ordered and the first that matches wins. The new route's page opens once it is saved.
tip.route.multipleAccounts: Yes: one browser may hold several signed-in accounts on this route and switch between them at /.iya-pep/accounts on the proxy. That page adds another account (a fresh sign-in, prompt=login), switches the active one, and signs one or all out here. Only the active account's identity is forwarded, after the same header stripping and the same XACML decision, and a CAEP session-revoked ends only the account it names. At most proxyMaxAccounts accounts per browser. Needs the session mechanism. No (the default): one sign-in per browser, as before.
tip.setting.proxyMaxAccounts: On a route with several accounts: the most accounts one browser may hold. A sign-in past it is refused (403) rather than signing another account out.
routePage.lead: One route of this PEP's reverse proxy. Every value of the route is edited in the form below, and saving checks the whole configuration exactly as the document editor on the Reverse proxy tab does. The PEP loads the change at its next poll.
routePage.notFound: {pep} has no route called {route}. It may have been renamed or removed.
routePage.usable: Yes: its application resolves, and the PEP serves the route.
routePage.publicUsable: Yes: a public route names no application, so it has nothing to resolve.
routePage.unusable: No: the PEP refuses this route (403) until its application qualifies.
routePage.noSuchApplication: No application with this identifier is in this realm's registry.
routePage.positionOf: {position} of {count} (0 is first; the first route whose path matches wins)
routePage.upstreamNote: The application behind the proxy is one URL for the whole PEP, not one per route, so it is not on this form. Change upstream in the configuration document on the Reverse proxy tab.
routePage.noListeners: The PEP has no reverse-proxy listener, so nothing serves this route.
routePage.applicationNote: The application this route fronts is chosen in the form above from this realm's registry; the current one is linked in the table above. A route that checks credentials must front one, so to clear it, make the route public.
routePage.publicIdentity: A public route establishes nobody, so it forwards no identity.
routePage.removeConfirm: Yes, remove {route} from this PEP's configuration
routePage.indexLead: Every route of every registered PEP's reverse proxy. Open one to edit it.
routePage.noRoutes: No registered PEP holds a reverse-proxy route in this realm.
tip.routePage.usable: Whether the PEP can serve the route now. A route whose application is missing or does not qualify for its mechanisms is refused (403) until it does. The reason is shown.
tip.routePage.upstream: Where the proxy forwards a request this route admits: the PEP's one upstream, with the request's path appended. The model has no per-route upstream.
tip.routePage.servedBy: Every reverse-proxy listener serves every route: the route table belongs to the proxy, not to a listener. Each row shows what the PEP last reported for that listener.
tip.routePage.rename: The route's id. Change it to rename the route: 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, not one another route of this PEP holds. The PEP serves the new id from its next poll. Until then, a request on this route may be refused while the PEP asks for the identity under the old id.
tip.peps.name: The name the PEP registered under. With a client certificate, it is the name of the directory entry the certificate is stored on, and PEP_NAME is ignored. Click it to open the PEP's own page.
tip.peps.certificate: The subject of the client certificate the PEP registered with. That certificate must be stored on exactly one directory entry, and the entry must hold REMOTE_PEPS. Unauthenticated means it proved nothing: it presented no certificate, and xacml.pepRequireCertificate is off.
tip.peps.state: Current: the PEP holds the policies this repository holds now (the same sync token). Stale: nothing has been heard from it for xacml.pepStaleAfterS seconds. A stale PEP may still be enforcing what it last pulled.
tip.peps.bias: What a decision that is not Permit or Deny means at that PEP. deny-biased: only Permit lets the request through. permit-biased: only Deny refuses it. Set by PEP_BIAS, or on the Settings tab.
tip.peps.enforced: Decisions the PEP reports making since it started: how many, how many it allowed and how many it refused. These are the PEP's own counts, carried on its heartbeat.
tip.peps.notify: The URL this service POSTs to when the policy repository changes, telling the PEP to pull now. The URL set on the Settings tab is used if there is one; otherwise the one the PEP registered with. It saves waiting for the next poll and does not replace the poll.
tip.peps.listener: The certificate this realm issued for the PEP's environment HTTPS listener (9443 and 9543). Only the PEP's own page can say whether that certificate is the one it is serving.
tip.peps.proxy: Whether a reverse-proxy configuration is set for this PEP, and how many routes it has. A route whose application no longer qualifies is refused by the PEP (403) and is flagged here.
tip.peps.actions: Stop nudging: this service stops POSTing to the PEP's notify URL. The PEP keeps pulling and enforcing. Forget: removes the register row only. A PEP that pulls again registers again.
tip.overview.name: The PEP's registered name: the directory entry its client certificate is stored on.
tip.overview.identity: The directory entry that certificate resolves to, the subject the REMOTE_PEPS role is checked on.
tip.overview.thumbprint: The SHA-256 thumbprint of the client certificate the PEP last registered with.
tip.overview.registered: When the PEP last registered. A registration keeps everything set on this page and drops what the PEP last reported.
tip.overview.version: The PEP's own version, M.N.O.build. The release always matches this service's.
tip.overview.description: What the PEP says it is: PEP_DESCRIPTION, or the description set on the Settings tab.
tip.overview.resource: The XACML resource id the PEP uses when a request names none: PEP_RESOURCE, or the resource set on the Settings tab.
tip.overview.syncToken: The sync token of the policies the PEP last pulled. When it equals the repository's, the PEP is current.
tip.overview.policies: How many enabled policies the PEP holds now.
tip.settings.setting: The setting, with the PEP environment variable it overrides.
tip.settings.setHere: The value this service sends the PEP. Not set means the PEP uses its environment variable, or the default if that is not set either. Saved values reach the PEP at its next poll.
tip.settings.inUse: The value the PEP reports it is using, and where that value came from: set here, its environment, or the default.
tip.settings.default: The value the PEP uses when neither this page nor its environment sets one.
tip.settings.applies: When a changed value takes effect at the PEP, after it has pulled the change.
tip.settings.variable: An environment variable this page cannot set. These are needed before the PEP's first pull, or they name a file on the PEP's own disk.
tip.settings.envDefault: The value the PEP uses when the variable is not set.
tip.settings.why: Why the variable stays in the PEP's environment.
tip.setting.description: What this PEP says it is, shown on its row and its page. Plain text.
tip.setting.resource: The XACML resource id a decision uses when the request names none, for example https://expenses.example.test. Empty: the request must name one.
tip.setting.notifyUrl: Where this service sends the nudge that tells the PEP to pull now: the PEP's HTTPS listener, for example https://xacml-pep:9443/notify. Only https is accepted; the nudge is never sent over plain http. A certificate this realm issued the PEP verifies with nothing else set. The nudge saves time; the poll still keeps the PEP up to date without it.
tip.setting.bias: What a decision that is neither Permit nor Deny means. deny-biased: only Permit lets the request through. permit-biased: only Deny refuses it.
tip.setting.pip: Ask this service's directory (POST /xacml/pip) for attributes a request did not carry, in one batched query before each evaluation. false: every attribute must be in the request.
tip.setting.pollIntervalMs: How often the PEP pulls the policies, the proxy configuration and these settings, in milliseconds. The PEP is guaranteed to converge at this interval. The nudge only makes it sooner.
tip.setting.heartbeatIntervalMs: How often the PEP reports its state (its counts, its listeners and the settings it is using), in milliseconds.
tip.setting.backoffMaxMs: The longest a refused poll or heartbeat waits before it tries again, in milliseconds. Each failure doubles the wait, up to this.
tip.setting.timeoutMs: How long a request to this service may take before the PEP gives up on it, in milliseconds.
tip.setting.maxBodyBytes: The largest request body the PEP's decision API and an AuthZEN evaluation accept, in bytes.
tip.setting.httpsReloadIntervalMs: How often the HTTPS listeners re-read PEP_HTTPS_CERT and PEP_HTTPS_KEY, in milliseconds. A new pair is served without a restart.
tip.setting.authzen: The AuthZEN edge PDP on the PEP's HTTPS listener. false answers 501.
tip.setting.authzenPdpIdentifier: The policy_decision_point named in the AuthZEN metadata: an https origin with no path, for example https://pep.example.test:9444. Empty: the origin each request arrived at.
tip.setting.authzenForwardTimeoutMs: How long an AuthZEN evaluation forwarded to this service may take before the caller gets 504, in milliseconds. Evaluations are forwarded for an application that enforces fine-grained authorization.
tip.setting.proxySessionRecheckMs: On a session route that does not use CAEP signals: how old this service's last "still signed in" answer may be before the next request asks again, in milliseconds. 0 asks on every request.
tip.setting.proxySessionTtlMs: The longest a proxy session lives, whatever this service says, in milliseconds. The default is 8 hours.
tip.setting.proxyMaxSessions: The most proxy sessions the PEP holds at once. A new sign-in past it is refused with 503.
tip.setting.proxyJwksTtlMs: How long the realm's JWKS is kept before it is fetched again, in milliseconds. 0 fetches it for every verification.
tip.setting.proxyUpstreamInsecure: Do not verify an https upstream's certificate. For development only.
tip.setting.proxyRpAllowInsecure: Let the session mechanism's relying party talk to an http issuer. For development only. Redirect URIs stay https.
tip.setting.proxySignalsPollMs: How often the CAEP/RISC receiver polls this service's signal stream, in milliseconds.
tip.setting.proxySignalsStaleMs: How long a signal stream may go without a successful poll, in milliseconds. After that, sessions are checked with this service's session endpoint instead.
tip.setting.proxyStripCookies: More cookies the reverse proxy never sends to the application, beside this service's own (its sign-on session's among them), which the proxy is told on every pull: names separated by commas, a trailing * matching a prefix, for example idp_session,sso_*. Leave it empty unless another identity provider shares the application's host. The application's own cookies are never removed unless named here.
tip.setting.facts: Values: {values}. Default: {default}. Takes effect {applies}. Precedence: a value set here wins over {env} in the PEP's environment, which wins over the default.
tip.setting.textValues: text of at most {max} characters, with no control character
tip.setting.urlValues: an absolute https URL (http only where this service allows it)
tip.listeners.listener: The listener's id. api-http, api-https, proxy-http and proxy-https are the four the PEP's environment binds, and those ids are reserved. The rest are defined on this tab.
tip.listeners.source: Environment: bound from the PEP's own variables, read-only here. Set here: defined on this tab, pulled with the settings, and bound at run time.
tip.listeners.address: The address and port the PEP reports it is bound to. Before it reports, the address and port in the listener's definition are shown.
tip.listeners.state: What the PEP last reported. Listening: it is serving. Waiting: an HTTPS listener with no certificate yet. Failed: the bind was refused, for the reason shown. Off: not bound on purpose.
tip.listeners.certificate: For HTTPS: the certificate the PEP reports it is serving, and the one this realm issued it. They differ until the PEP picks up a renewal.
tip.listeners.actions: Remove unbinds the listener at the PEP's next poll. Renew makes the PEP generate a new key and ask for a new certificate. The environment's four change only in its environment.
tip.listener.id: A name for the listener, unique on this PEP: 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, for example public-https. api-http, api-https, proxy-http and proxy-https are reserved. It cannot be changed once saved: remove the listener and add it again.
tip.listener.protocol: HTTPS: the PEP generates the key, and this realm's Remote PEP listeners CA (pep-tls) certifies it, so no private key reaches this service. HTTP: plain text. In product mode a plain-HTTP proxy listener also needs xacml.pepPlainHttpProxyListeners.
tip.listener.purpose: What the listener serves. The decision API: GET /, /protected, /notify, /healthcheck, and AuthZEN over HTTPS. The reverse proxy: the route table on the Reverse proxy tab.
tip.listener.address: The local address to bind: 0.0.0.0 for every IPv4 address, :: for every IPv6 address, or one of the PEP's own, for example 10.0.0.5. Default 0.0.0.0.
tip.listener.port: 1 to 65535, for example 8443. A port another listener holds is refused. That includes an environment listener the PEP reports in use. One the PEP reports off holds no port.
tip.listener.dnsNames: HTTPS only. Up to 16 DNS names the certificate carries, separated by commas or spaces, for example pep.example.test, pep.internal. The PEP's registered name is always included. A change makes a new key and certificate.
tip.listener.ipAddresses: HTTPS only. IP addresses the certificate carries, for example 10.0.0.5. A change makes a new key and certificate.
tip.listener.keyAlg: HTTPS only. The key the PEP generates: ec-p256 (the default), ec-p384, rsa-2048 or rsa-3072. A change makes a new key and certificate.
tip.listener.when: A saved definition is pulled with the settings, and the PEP binds, rebinds or unbinds the listener at its next poll. No restart is needed.
tip.issue.dnsNames: More DNS names for the PEP's environment HTTPS pair (9443 and 9543), separated by commas, for example pep.example.test. The PEP's registered name and the host of its notify URL are always included.
tip.issue.ipAddresses: IP addresses the pair carries, separated by commas, for example 10.0.0.5.
tip.issue.keyAlg: The key this service generates for the pair. The private key is in this reply only, once. Write it to PEP_HTTPS_KEY and the chain to PEP_HTTPS_CERT, and the PEP serves the pair within PEP_HTTPS_RELOAD_INTERVAL_MS. Issuing again replaces the pair and revokes the old certificate as superseded.
tip.routes.id: The route's id. Click it to open the route's own page, where every value can be edited.
tip.routes.path: The path the route matches, and how: prefix (the path and everything under it) or exact.
tip.routes.methods: The methods the route takes. Any means every method. Another method on a matching path is refused with 405.
tip.routes.mechanisms: How a caller proves who they are on this route. Public: nobody is asked and no policy is consulted.
tip.routes.application: The application in this realm's registry the route fronts. A route whose application does not qualify is refused (403) until it does.
tip.routes.decision: What the XACML decision is asked about: the route's resource and action, or the request's path and method when they are empty.
tip.routes.headers: How the identity reaches the application: the headers and the claims they carry, or a SAML assertion, or a JWT.
tip.routes.forward: Whether the caller's own Authorization header and cookies are forwarded to the application.
tip.routes.actions: Remove deletes the route from the configuration. The PEP stops serving it at its next poll.
tip.route.id: The route's id, unique in this PEP's configuration: 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, for example orders-api. The PEP's identity requests and the signal streams name the route by it.
tip.route.path: The request path the route matches. It starts with /, for example /api or /orders/export, and holds no //, %, \, ?, #, space, or . or .. segment. With prefix, /api matches /api and /api/x but not /apix. / matches everything.
tip.route.match: prefix (the default): the path and everything under it, at a / boundary. exact: that path only. The routes are tried in order, and the first whose path matches wins.
tip.route.methods: The HTTP methods the route takes, for example GET and HEAD for a read-only path, or GET and POST for a form. None ticked takes any method. Another method on a matching path is refused with 405. The next route is not tried.
tip.route.public: Yes: no credential is asked for and no policy is consulted, and the request is forwarded as it is. A public route names no mechanism, no application and no identity. Default no.
tip.route.mechanisms: How a caller proves who they are; any one ticked will do. session: a browser signs in at this service as the application's OIDC client. oauth2: a Bearer access token for the application's audience. saml2: a SAML assertion for its SP entity ID. basic: a username and an app password. A route that is not public needs at least one.
tip.route.application: The identifier of the application in this realm's registry (Directory → Applications) the route fronts, for example orders-app. Required unless the route is public. The token audience, the SAML entity ID and the OIDC client are read from its entry at each pull, and a save refuses one that does not qualify.
tip.route.resource: The XACML resource id the decision asks about, for example https://orders.example.test. Empty: the request's path, for example /orders/42.
tip.route.action: The XACML action id, for example read. Empty: the request's method, for example GET.
tip.route.forward: Yes: the caller's own Authorization header and cookies are forwarded to the application. No (the default): they are removed, and only the identity the route's identity mode sends reaches the application.
tip.route.signals: Yes (the default): on a session route, the CAEP session-revoked signal from this service's stream ends the proxy session at once. No: the PEP asks this service whether the session is still live, at most every proxySessionRecheckMs.
tip.route.position: Where the route goes in the list, from 0 (first) to the number of routes. The first route whose path matches wins, so put a narrower path before a wider one. Empty keeps an edited route where it is and puts a new one last.
tip.route.when: Saving validates the whole configuration with the same checks as the document editor. The PEP loads it at its next poll, or at once when it is nudged.
tip.identity.mode: How the identity reaches the application. headers: claims in request headers you name. saml: a SAML assertion this service issues for the application, posted to its registered ACS. jwt: an access token this service issues for the application's audience, sent as Authorization: Bearer. Default headers with none, which forwards no identity.
tip.identity.headerName: The request header a claim is sent in, an RFC 9110 token, for example X-Remote-User. Up to 16, unique regardless of case. Authorization, Cookie, Host, Forwarded, X-Forwarded-* and hop-by-hop headers are refused. The proxy removes every configured header from the incoming request first, so a client cannot inject one.
tip.identity.claim: The claim the header carries: sub, username, email, name, given_name, family_name, groups, mechanism, acr or amr. A row with no claim is left out.
tip.identity.separator: Joins a claim that has several values (groups, amr): one printable character that is not a letter or digit. Default ,.
tip.proxy.document: The whole configuration as JSON: enabled, upstream (the one application behind the proxy, an absolute http(s) URL such as http://app.internal:8080), publicBaseUrl (where browsers reach the proxy, for the session sign-in), upstreamTimeoutMs, maxBodyBytes and routes. A save validates it whole, and a refusal names the member. The PEP loads it at its next poll.
tip.signals.serves: The applications and routes the stream's OIDC client serves on this PEP.
tip.signals.stream: The stream's id at this service's transmitter.
tip.signals.lastPoll: When the receiver last polled, whether or not the poll succeeded.
tip.signals.lastSuccess: When a poll last succeeded. A stream with no success for proxySignalsStaleMs is stale.
tip.signals.failures: Failed polls in a row since the last success.
tip.signals.polls: Polls made, and how many of them failed.
tip.signals.sets: Security event tokens accepted, and refused (for example, one whose signature did not verify).
tip.signals.ended: Proxy sessions this stream has ended, through CAEP session-revoked or a RISC event.
tip.signals.health: Healthy: the last poll succeeded within proxySignalsStaleMs. Stale: it did not, and sessions are checked with this service's session endpoint until it does.
proxy.signals.oldest: Oldest successful poll {age} ms before the report; at most {failures} failure(s) in a row.
proxy.signals.neverPolled: No stream has polled yet; at most {failures} failure(s) in a row.
proxy.signals.sets: {accepted} SET(s) accepted, {refused} refused; {ended} session(s) ended by a signal.
